summary: Standards-track Telnet option that lets a client and server exchange the type of terminal in use, so the server can format output properly. It supersedes RFC 930, and adds the ability to cycle through a list of possible terminal types to select the most appropriate one.

plainLanguage.summary:
Telnet clients on modern hardware usually pretend to be several different terminals at once. The server has to be told which one to use, or its output will look wrong.

This option is the negotiation for that. The server asks, the client answers with a name, and the server can ask again to get the next name on the client's list. When the same name comes back twice, the list has run out. The rule is deliberately one-sided: only the server asks, because a server cannot change its terminal type mid-session.

subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a server ask the client which kind of terminal it is emulating.

tldr.problem: A modern client usually emulates several kinds of terminal at once, and the server needs to know which one to talk to. The earlier Telnet option allowed only one name, treated several names as synonyms, and could be scanned only once.
tldr.mechanism: The option keeps the familiar negotiation, with the server asking and the client answering, and adds a way to walk down a list. The client sends a different name each time it is asked, and repeats the last name to signal the end of the list.
tldr.outcome: A server that does not understand the first name can ask again and get the next one, so the client can offer a choice in preference order. The RFC supersedes RFC 930 and keeps the old behaviour working by assuming one thing about implementations built to the previous standard.

facts.label: Maximum length of a terminal type name

today: RFC 1091 is a Proposed Standard from February 1989. It supersedes RFC 930 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document states that it assumes one thing about implementations built to the previous standard, namely that such a client answers a third query with the last type on its list, so that the two kinds of implementation can be mixed.

sections.title: The Option and Its Commands
sections.content:
The option is called TERMINAL-TYPE and has the code 24. Its four negotiation commands carry the usual meanings. WILL means the sender is willing to send terminal type information in a subsequent sub-negotiation, WON'T means the sender refuses to send it, DO means the sender is willing to receive it in a subsequent sub-negotiation, and DON'T means the sender refuses to accept it.

Two sub-commands carry the information itself. IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE SEND IAC SE means the server requests the client to transmit his next terminal type and to switch emulation mode if more than one terminal type is supported; the code for SEND is 1. IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE IS ... IAC SE means the client is stating the name of his current or only terminal type; the code for IS is 0.

The default state is that terminal type information is not exchanged: the default for the sending side is WON'T TERMINAL-TYPE and the default for the receiving side is DON'T TERMINAL-TYPE.
sections.plainLanguage: Four commands agree whether to talk about terminal types at all, and two sub-commands do the talking. The default is not to talk about them.

sections.title: Why the Option Exists
sections.content:
On most machines with bit-mapped displays, such as personal computers and graphics workstations, a client terminal emulation program is used to simulate a conventional ASCII terminal. Most of these programs have multiple emulation modes, frequently with widely varying characteristics. Likewise, modern host system software and applications can deal with a variety of terminal types.

What is needed is a means for the client to present a list of available terminal emulation modes to the server, from which the server can select the one it prefers, for arbitrary reasons. There is also a need for a mechanism to change emulation modes during the course of a session, perhaps according to the needs of application programs.

The existing terminal-type passing mechanisms within Telnet were not designed with multiple emulation modes in mind. While multiple names are allowed, they are assumed to be synonyms. Emulation mode changes are not defined, and the list of modes can only be scanned once. This document defines a simple extension to the existing mechanisms which meets both criteria, and it makes one assumption about the behaviour of implementations coded to the previous standard in order to obtain full backwards compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem was not just naming the terminal. A client could offer several terminal types, but the server could not ask for the next one after rejecting the first, and there was no way to say that the client had switched to a different one.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
Willingness to exchange terminal-type information is agreed through conventional Telnet option negotiation. WILL and DO are used only to obtain and grant permission for future discussion; the actual exchange happens within the option sub-commands.

Once the two hosts have exchanged a WILL and a DO, the sender of the DO, which is the server, is free to request type information. Only the server may send requests and only the client may transmit actual type information. Terminal type information may not be sent spontaneously, but only in response to a request.

The terminal type information is an NVT ASCII string, within which upper and lower case are considered equivalent. The complete list of valid terminal type names is kept in the latest Assigned Numbers document.

The transmission of terminal type information by the client implies that the client must simultaneously change emulation mode, unless the type sent is a synonym of the preceding type, or there are other prerequisites for entering the new regime, such as having agreed the Telnet binary option. The receipt of such information by the server does not imply any immediate change of processing, but the information may be passed to a process, which may alter the data it sends to suit the characteristics of the terminal. Some operating systems have a terminal driver that accepts a code indicating the type of terminal being driven, and by using the TERMINAL TYPE and BINARY options a Telnet server on such a system could arrange to have terminals driven as if they were directly connected, including special functions not available to a standard Network Virtual Terminal.

The specification is deliberately asymmetric. It is assumed that server operating systems and applications in general cannot change terminal types at arbitrary points in a session, so the client may only send a new type, and potentially change emulation modes, when the server requests that it do so.
sections.plainLanguage: Answering the server also means switching the emulator to match the name sent. The server does not have to act immediately, but it may pass the name to the program that produces the output so that it can format things for that terminal.

sections.title: Cycling Through a List of Terminal Types
sections.content:
The terminal type information may be any NVT ASCII string meaningful to both ends of the negotiation. The list of terminal type names in the Assigned Numbers document is intended to minimize confusion caused by alternative spellings, because confusion would arise if one party called a terminal one thing and the other called it another. There is no negative acknowledgement for a terminal type that is not understood, but other options, such as switching to binary mode, may be refused if a valid terminal type name has not been specified.

In some cases a particular terminal may be known by more than one name, for example a specific type and a more generic type, or the client may be a workstation with an integrated display capable of emulating more than one kind of terminal. In such cases the sender of the IS command should reply to successive SEND commands with the various names, so that a server that does not understand the first response can prompt for alternatives. If different terminal emulations are supported by the client, the mode of the emulator must be changed to match the last type sent, unless that emulation has other Telnet options as prerequisites, in which case the emulation switches when the prerequisite is fulfilled. When types are synonyms they should be sent in order from most to least specific.

When the server receives the same response two consecutive times, that indicates the end of the list of available types. Similarly, the client should indicate that it has sent all available names by repeating the last one sent. If an additional request is received, that indicates the server wishes to return to the top of the list of available types, probably to select the least of N evils.

Server implementations conforming to the previous standard will cease sending SEND commands after receiving the same response two consecutive times, which works according to the old standard. It is assumed that client implementations conforming to the previous standard will send the last type on the list in response to a third query as well as the second, and new-style servers must recognise this and not send more queries.

The type UNKNOWN should be used if the type of the terminal is unknown or unlikely to be recognized by the other party. The complete and up-to-date list of terminal type names is maintained in the Assigned Numbers document, and the maximum length of a terminal type name is 40 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The client offers its terminal types in order of preference, and repeats the last one to say that is all of them. The server walks down the list until it finds one it understands.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first example is the simplest case, where the server finds the first type acceptable. The server sends DO TERMINAL-TYPE and the client replies WILL TERMINAL-TYPE, after which the server may request a terminal type at any time. The server then sends SEND and the client answers with IS and the name IBM-3278-2.

The second example is compatible with the previous standard. The server asks and the client answers with ZENITH-H19. The server asks again and the client answers with UNKNOWN. The server asks a third time and the client answers with UNKNOWN again, which is how the end of the list is signalled.

The third example is the new behaviour, where the server requests additional terminal types and proceeds beyond the end of the list to select the first type offered by the client. The client offers DEC-VT220, then DEC-VT100, then DEC-VT52, then repeats DEC-VT52 to mark the end of the list, and after one more request from the server it starts again with DEC-VT220.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the three cases: the server takes the first name offered, the server takes the last name on an old-style list, and the server walks past the end of the list and comes back round to the first.

viz.caption: The rules that make the exchange work

items.title: Asymmetric by design
items.text: Only the server may ask and only the client may answer, because server operating systems and applications cannot change terminal types at arbitrary points in a session.

items.title: No spontaneous messages
items.text: Terminal type information may not be sent except in response to a request.

items.title: Case does not matter
items.text: The terminal type information is an NVT ASCII string, and upper and lower case are considered equivalent.

items.title: One spelling
items.text: The list of valid names is kept in the Assigned Numbers document, to avoid confusion caused by different spellings of the same terminal.

items.title: Unknown
items.text: The type UNKNOWN should be used if the type of the terminal is unknown or unlikely to be recognized by the other party.

viz.caption: How the client walks down its list

items.title: Repeat to end the list
items.text: When the server receives the same response twice in a row, the list of available types has ended.

items.title: Synonyms go from specific to general
items.text: When types are synonyms, they should be sent in order from most to least specific.

items.title: Repeating the last one ends it
items.text: The client should indicate that it has sent all available names by repeating the last one sent.

items.title: Going past the end wraps around
items.text: An additional request after the end means the server wants to return to the top of the list.

items.title: Old servers stop at the repeat
items.text: A server built to the previous standard stops sending requests after receiving the same response twice, which works under the old rules too.

items.title: New servers must not query again
items.text: A client built to the previous standard answers the third query with the last type on its list, and a new-style server has to recognise that and stop.
